summary: Wooden fire tower at Bolton Valley Resort at 3,150 ft, reached by a hiking trail; an 1922 steel tower on Bolton Mountain may be a different structure.

access.note: Reached on foot from Bolton Valley Resort; hiking access is free.

visit.trail_note: 3.1-mile out-and-back Vista Peak trail from near The Backcountry and Nordic Center; parking near the main base lodge.

events.note: Steel tower on the summit of Bolton Mountain, donated by C.D. Ordway and largely built by Ralph Dunsmoor. The entry ends with the word Removed. Not confirmed as the same site as the present wooden tower.

evidence.supports: climb via the Vista Lookout Tower Trail at Bolton Valley Resort, with views from the top
evidence.quote: Climb Vista Lookout Tower Trail at Bolton Valley Resort to take in the view from the top of this tower

evidence.supports: parking near the main base lodge
evidence.quote: Parking is available at Bolton Valley Resort near the main base lodge.

evidence.supports: views of Camel's Hump and Mount Mansfield
evidence.quote: including Camel’s Hump to the south and Mount Mansfield to the north

evidence.supports: only known surviving wooden fire tower in Vermont, at Bolton Valley
evidence.quote: just one known wooden tower survives, at Bolton Valley.

evidence.supports: steel tower donated by C.D. Ordway
evidence.quote: This was a steel windmill tower and was donated by C.D. Ordway.
The work was in charge of, and largely done by Ralph Dunsmoor.

evidence.supports: state forestry department and Burlington section of the Green Mountain Club helped pay
evidence.quote: The cost of erecting this tower was assumed partly by the State club, by the Burlington section of the Green Mountain club, by the State forestry department and by several private donations.

evidence.supports: the entry ends with the word Removed
Vista Peak trail is a 3.1-mile out-and-back hike from near The Backcountry and Nordic Center
evidence.quote: The Vista Peak Trail begins near The Backcountry and Nordic Center and is a 3.1-mile out-and-back hike.

corrections.why: The OpenStreetMap ele tag reads 3200 with no unit. The cited guide gives the tower's elevation as 3,150 feet, which is about 960 metres. The record's metre value is about three times too high.

sources.title: 14 Fire Towers to Climb in Vermont
Watching from above: The story of Vermont's fire towers
5 Fire Towers to Climb for Vermont Fall Foliage Views

notes_for_editor: Current tower's build date, builder, height and condition are unknown. The 1922 steel tower on Bolton Mountain may or may not be the same site: the Forest Lookouts entry ends with Removed, and the Chronicle describes the surviving tower as wooden. A 1921 newspaper quote gives the mountain as 3,600 with no unit, which does not match 3,150 ft; left unresolved. The OSM ele tag of 3200 is proposed for correction to metres. Guides disagree on how many Vermont towers still stand (14 in one, about twenty in the Chronicle). Ask Bolton Valley Resort whether the tower is open to climb before any visit.
